1.profile:
Oversharing does not require a hack. It can start with a link that was a little too convenient.

In SharePoint Online, a file can be reachable through site permissions, through a Microsoft 365 group, or through a sharing link. An organization-wide or anonymous link can quietly widen access far beyond the people you had in mind.

That matters more now, because AI assistants like Copilot can surface what a user is able to open.

You do not need a big project to begin. Pick one sensitive site, check who sits in Owners, Members and Visitors, and look at which link types are used for files and folders.

1.page:
Oversharing means content in Microsoft 365 is shared more broadly than intended, for example through organization-wide or anonymous links.

In SharePoint Online, access comes from two layers: site permissions (a Microsoft 365 group or the Owners, Members and Visitors groups) and sharing links for single files and folders. Both can widen access over time.

Because most files shared in Teams are stored in SharePoint, these permissions also decide what Copilot can find for a user.

The article explains the mechanics and gives a short checklist for a first review.

1.group:
A question for the admins here: when you hear "oversharing", do you think of permissions or of sharing links?

In SharePoint Online both matter. Site permissions give access to everything in a site, while Anyone, People in your organization and Specific people links open up single files and folders. A broad link can undo careful site design, and AI assistants like Copilot can surface whatever a user is able to open.

2.profile:
One entry in a permissions list can make a whole site visible to every internal user: "Everyone except external users".

It is easy to miss because it looks like a harmless group name. But granting it access to a site or library means every internal user in your tenant can reach that content, at whatever level you granted.

That is one reason it deserves a look before you roll out AI assistants like Copilot, which can surface what users can already access.

A practical start: check which sites and libraries contain this claim, and compare that with who actually needs access. Do this review in a pilot area first, and have a way back before you change any permissions.

2.page:
"Everyone except external users" is a built-in claim that includes every internal user of a tenant.

If it is granted access to a site or library, that content becomes broadly visible inside the organization. This is a common source of oversharing, and AI assistants like Copilot can surface content that users already have permission to see.

The article explains how the claim differs from Microsoft 365 group membership and from sharing links, and what to check first. Any permission change should be tested on a pilot site and have a way back.

3.profile:
A file can be open to every colleague without anyone having decided that on purpose.

One common cause is a link or permission that targets "Everyone except external users". It is easy to create and easy to forget, and it matters more once AI assistants like Copilot can surface content to people who have access.

Microsoft Learn describes two built-in ways to look for it: data access governance reports in the SharePoint admin center, and a CSV report for a single site. Both have limits you should know before you rely on them.

The article walks through where to look, what the reports leave out, and a sensible order for cleaning up.

3.page:
Where do you find files that are shared with everyone? Microsoft Learn documents two built-in options.

Data access governance reports in the SharePoint admin center cover the whole organization, including content shared with "Everyone except external users". They need SharePoint Advanced Management and the SharePoint administrator role.

A site admin can also create a CSV report for one site or OneDrive. It does not include Anyone links or links that were e-mailed but not clicked.

The article explains what each report covers, what it misses, and how to work through the results safely.

3.group:
Question for the group: how do you find content that is open to the whole organization?

The built-in options each have a gap. The admin center reports need SharePoint Advanced Management. The single-site CSV report leaves out Anyone links and links that were e-mailed but not clicked, and it shows SharePoint groups without the people inside them.

That means one report rarely gives the full picture, and the cleanup itself needs care because changing permissions can break access that people rely on.
